Abidjan (port locode CIABJ) is the principal seaport, the largest city and the economic capital of the Ivory Coast (Cote d'Ivoire). It is also one of Africa's most populous French-speaking cities. The city has population around 4,4 million.

Considered Africa's cultural crossroad, Abidjan is characterized by a high level of urbanization and industrialization. The city quickly expanded after a new dock/wharf was built in 1931, and in 1933 it was designated as the capital of the then-French colony. Abidjan City remained Ivory Coast's capital after the country gained its independence from France in 1960.

After the Vridi Canal was completed in 1951, the city also became a major seaport. In 1983, Yamoussoukro was designated as Cote d'Ivoire's official capital. However, nearly all foreign embassies and political institutions remained in Abidjan City (designated as the country's "economic capital"). The encompassing Abidjan Autonomous District (plus some city suburbs) is one of Ivory Coast's all 14 districts.

By shipping traffic volumes, Port Abidjan is ranked West Africa's largest seaport and Africa's second-largest, after Lagos (Nigeria). The containership/cargo port was opened in 1951. The largest ships dock in the Vridi Canal which has draft 15 m (50 ft).

Abidjan City is the economic center of the Ivory Coast and as well as of the inland countries Mali and Burkina Faso. The city's road infrastructure effectively increased the seaport's activities as ~50% of the businesses based in Burkina Faso, Niger and Mali pass through it. Port Abidjan receives ~60% of ivory park industry. It also serves the region's oil production (especially refining and distribution) and cargo exports (cocoa, coffee, bananas, pineapples, cashew, mango, manganese, timber).

In August 2020 was signed a contract with CHEC (China Harbour Engineering Company) for the construction of the new Cote d’Ivoire Terminal - port’s second container terminal. Works started on October 5, 2020, and are scheduled for completion by the end of 2021. The new facility is adjacent to Abidjan Terminal (port's first) and both are operated by a joint venture company formed by Bollore Ports (port infrastructure operator and logistics company) and APM Terminals (The Hague Holland-based port and container terminal operator/one of the world's largest). Abidjan's new container terminal will increase seaport's annual capacity with 1,2 million TEU-containers (annually). Cote d’Ivoire Terminal covers total area 37,5 hectares (93 acres/~0,4 km2) and is well-connected with the city.

On November 2, 2022, was officially opened/became fully operational Port Abidjan's Cote d'Ivoire Terminal. The facility is a joint venture between APM Terminals (Netherlands) and Bollore Ports (South Africa/part of Bollore Group). The new terminal's first vessel was the 6000-TEU boxship CMA CGM ROSSINI (2004-built, IMO 9280639).

Abidjan is primarily an excursion-oriented cruise port rather than a walk-off destination. Ships dock alongside inside the large commercial Port of Abidjan, and recent cruise calls have frequently used the new Grain Terminal. The port is an industrial, controlled area, so passengers should not expect to walk directly from the ship into the city. For most visitors, a cruise excursion or a pre-arranged vehicle with driver is the practical way to explore.

At a Glance

  • Independent sightseeing: Organized excursion recommended, although independent touring is possible with a pre-arranged driver.
  • Dock or tender: Ships normally dock alongside.
  • Walk from the ship: Not practical; the berth is inside a working commercial port.
  • Best short-call option: A guided or private-driver tour of central Abidjan and Le Plateau.
  • Best longer excursion: Historic Grand-Bassam or Banco National Park.
  • Public transport: Not recommended for a time-limited cruise visit.

Getting from the Cruise Port

Abidjan does not have a conventional downtown cruise terminal surrounded by tourist facilities. Recent large cruise ships have used the port's Grain Terminal, a 700 m (0.4 mi) quay commissioned in 2023, although the exact berth can vary between calls.

The port complex is separated from Abidjan's main sightseeing areas by industrial roads and the Ébrié Lagoon. Le Plateau, the central business district, is roughly 5 km (3.1 mi) from the port area, but driving time can vary considerably with traffic.

Do not assume that taxis or ride-hailing vehicles can collect passengers directly beside the ship. Cruise-line coaches and locally arranged tours commonly meet inside the controlled port area. Independent visitors should confirm the authorized meeting point with the ship before arranging a driver.

For independent travel, a pre-arranged private car or reputable ride-hailing service is preferable to shared taxis or minibuses. Abidjan traffic can be heavy and unpredictable, particularly around bridges and major junctions.

Best Ways to Spend Your Time

Le Plateau and Central Abidjan

Allow 3–4 hours. This is the most realistic introduction to Abidjan during a shorter call. Le Plateau contains the city's high-rise business district and several notable modern buildings, including St Paul's Cathedral with its distinctive concrete bell tower and stained glass.

A driver or guided city tour is preferable to trying to reach the district by public transport. Once dropped in Le Plateau, short sections can be explored on foot during daylight, but it is better to have transport available between stops rather than plan a long city walk.

The Musée des Civilisations de Côte d'Ivoire is also in Le Plateau, but it is currently listed as temporarily closed. Check locally before including it in a port-day itinerary.

Banco National Park

Allow about 4–5 hours including transfers. Banco National Park protects tropical forest within the Abidjan metropolitan area and offers walking through dense vegetation close to the city. It has repeatedly featured in sightseeing programs arranged for visiting cruise ships.

This is not a practical destination to approach casually from the port. Arrange a vehicle and preferably a guide in advance. Trails can be hot, humid and muddy after rain, so closed footwear, water and insect protection are useful.

Historic Grand-Bassam

Allow at least 5–6 hours. Grand-Bassam is approximately 35 km (21.7 mi) by road from the Treichville side of Abidjan. In light traffic the drive can take around 30–40 minutes, but cruise passengers should plan for substantially longer when congestion is possible.

The UNESCO-listed historic quarter preserves the former colonial administrative town between the lagoon and Atlantic Ocean. Typical visits include the historic streets, old administrative buildings and the National Costume Museum. The town also has Atlantic beaches, although a cruise visit is better focused on the historic district unless plenty of time is available.

Organized excursion recommended. The distance and variable road traffic make a ship excursion or pre-arranged private tour more appropriate than local public transport.

Bingerville Botanical Garden

Allow about 4 hours. The botanical garden at Bingerville is another established cruise-excursion destination and provides a quieter alternative to central Abidjan. Its mature tropical vegetation makes it suitable for passengers interested in nature without committing to a longer forest walk.

Use organized or pre-arranged transport. It can be combined with a limited Abidjan city tour on a longer call, but attempting to combine Bingerville, Banco and Grand-Bassam in one normal port day would involve too much road travel.

Is a Self-Guided Walking Tour Practical?

A port-to-city walking tour is not recommended. The ship berths inside an operational commercial port, the sightseeing districts are separated from the docks by busy roads, and the main attractions are spread across a large metropolitan area.

Short daytime walks within Le Plateau are possible after arriving by vehicle, for example around St Paul's Cathedral and nearby central landmarks. However, Abidjan is better treated as a driving-and-stops destination than as a continuous walking city during a cruise call.

Practical Tips

  • Confirm the day's berth and passenger exit arrangements on board; cruise ships do not necessarily use exactly the same quay on every visit.
  • Do not plan to walk out through the commercial port unless the ship specifically confirms that pedestrian access is permitted.
  • For independent sightseeing, arrange a reputable driver and a clear port pickup point before going ashore.
  • Ride-hailing or pre-arranged private taxis are preferable to informal shared transport. Public buses and minibuses are poor choices when ship-return time is critical.
  • Keep valuables discreet and remain alert in crowded streets and markets. Avoid walking around the city after dark.
  • Photography around the port, government buildings and other sensitive installations can be restricted; ask before taking photographs.
  • Allow a generous return margin. Abidjan traffic can significantly increase journey times, especially when crossing the lagoon or returning from Grand-Bassam.
  • For a call of only a few hours, stay within Abidjan. Grand-Bassam and more distant sights are better suited to a longer port stay or an organized excursion with controlled timing.
